### CANDIDATE DETAIL
#### 1. infantile convulsions and choreoathetosis  —  Tier 1 — Definitive / Highly Plausible  (fitness 0.783)
**Link type:** shared causal gene (HGNC:30500)

**Proposed mechanism:** PRRT2 (HGNC:30500) —LEADS_TO→ Seizures (HP:0001250); PRRT2 (HGNC:30500) —LEADS_TO→ Choreoathetosis (HP:0002067); PRRT2 (HGNC:30500) —LEADS_TO→ Paroxysmal dyskinesia (HP:0002343). Loss-of-function mutations in PRRT2 lead to both seizures and choreoathetosis in infantile convulsions and choreoathetosis, and also to paroxysmal dyskinesia in paroxysmal kinesigenic dyskinesia, demonstrating a shared genetic origin.

**How to falsify it:** Identification of pathogenic variants in PRRT2 that lead to gain-of-function or dominant-negative effects in one of the diseases, while the other is associated with loss-of-function, would falsify the shared loss-of-function mechanism. _(variant: High frequency (>= 1%) of pathogenic variants associated with either disease in gnomAD.)_

**Why it matters:** Understanding the shared role of PRRT2 in these neurological disorders could lead to unified therapeutic strategies targeting the underlying molecular pathways, potentially benefiting patients with either condition.

#### 2. episodic kinesigenic dyskinesia 1  —  Tier 1 — Definitive / Highly Plausible  (fitness 0.730)
**Link type:** shared causal gene (HGNC:30500)

**Proposed mechanism:** PRRT2 (HGNC:30500) —DISRUPTS→ neuronal excitability regulation (GO:0007212); neuronal excitability regulation (GO:0007212) —LEADS_TO→ paroxysmal dyskinesia (HP:0002374); neuronal excitability regulation (GO:0007212) —LEADS_TO→ dystonia (HP:0001317). Loss-of-function variants in PRRT2 disrupt neuronal excitability regulation, leading to paroxysmal dyskinesia and dystonia.

**How to falsify it:** Discovery of individuals with MONDO:0011593 or episodic kinesigenic dyskinesia 1 caused by variants in genes other than PRRT2, or by gain-of-function variants in PRRT2. _(variant: rs147279185)_

**Why it matters:** Understanding the role of PRRT2 in neuronal excitability may lead to targeted therapies for these movement disorders, potentially involving modulation of neurotransmitter release or ion channel function.
